# Zika virus infection

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Zoonoses and vector-borne diseases > Zika virus infection*

[Original Article Link](/library/Xo090S)

---

## Summary

<u>Zika virus</u> is an <u>arbovirus</u> that is primarily transmitted by the mosquito <u>Aedes aegypti</u>; transmission can also occur transplacentally and sexually. <u>Epidemic</u> <u>outbreaks</u> of <u>Zika virus</u> infection have occurred in South America, US territories, and certain southern US states. Patients often have no or mild <u>flu-like symptoms</u>. However, infection during <u>pregnancy</u> can result in <u>congenital Zika syndrome</u>. Diagnostic confirmation with <u>NAAT</u> is recommended for pregnant patients with a potential <u>Zika virus</u> infection. Treatment is primarily symptomatic, as there is currently no curative therapy.

---

## Epidemiology

* Worldwide geographical distribution [[1]](/library/JwWsPn0)

* <u>Outbreaks</u> most commonly occur in tropical and subtropical regions.

* Before 2015, a few cases were reported in Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific islands.

* Since 2015, <u>epidemic</u> <u>outbreaks</u> have been reported in South America (especially Brazil).

* <u>Epidemiology</u> in the US

* Almost all reported cases are acquired during travel to <u>endemic</u> regions.   [[2]](/library/qwWCPn0)

* During the 2016 <u>outbreak</u>: [[3]](/library/k9Wmnn0)

* Most locally-acquired cases were reported in US territories (e.g., Puerto Rico).

* Approximately 4000 cases were reported in the continental US, mostly in New York, Florida, California, and Texas.




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Zika virus</u>

* Genus: <u>flavivirus</u>, type of <u>arbovirus</u>

* <u>Positive-sense</u>, single-stranded, enveloped <u>RNA</u>

* Route of transmission

* <u>Vector-borne transmission</u> by the mosquito <u>Aedes aegypti</u> (common)

* Bite during the daytime

* Can also transmit other infections, e.g., <u>dengue</u>, <u>yellow fever</u>, and <u>chikungunya</u>

* Transplacental transmission from the mother to the fetus

* Sexual transmission

## Clinical features

* Incubation: 2–14 days

* Approx. 80% of cases remain asymptomatic

* In symptomatic patients, the manifestations are usually mild and last for 2–7 days.

* Low-grade <u>fever</u>

* <u>Flu-like</u> symptoms: <u>headache</u>, <u>arthralgia</u>, <u>myalgia</u>, non-<u>purulent</u> <u>conjunctivitis</u>, <u>malaise</u>

* <u>Maculopapular</u>, pruritic <u>rash</u> (20% of cases) [[6]](/library/F0bg3H)





> [!NOTE]
> The symptoms of <u>Zika virus</u> infection in adults are usually mild and non-specific, but its complications may be devastating (see “Complications” below).




References:[[7]](/library/LSawZ4)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[1]](/library/JwWsPn0)[[2]](/library/qwWCPn0)




* Suspect Zika infection based on symptoms and relevant <u>vector</u> or sexual exposure.

* Within 2 weeks of travel to an area with an <u>outbreak</u> or <u>sexual activity</u> with a person who has recently been in an area with an <u>outbreak</u> [[8]](/library/swWt4n0)

* Up to 12 weeks after symptom onset in a pregnant patient [[8]](/library/swWt4n0)

* Routine lab findings are nonspecific but may include <u>thrombocytopenia</u> and <u>leukopenia</u>. [[8]](/library/swWt4n0)

* Order diagnostic confirmation for patients who are pregnant and have either:

* Clinical features of Zika infection

* A <u>prenatal ultrasound</u> with findings of <u>congenital Zika syndrome</u>

* For patients with <u>vector</u> exposure, exclude <u>dengue infection</u>.  [[2]](/library/qwWCPn0)





> [!TIP]
> For symptomatic nonpregnant patients who have traveled to an area with an <u>outbreak</u> within the previous 2 weeks, perform only <u>dengue diagnostics</u>; diagnostic testing for <u>Zika virus</u> is not recommended. [[2]](/library/qwWCPn0)




### Diagnostic confirmation [[2]](/library/qwWCPn0)




* <u>NAAT</u> (e.g., <u>RT-PCR</u>) to detect viral <u>RNA</u>

* Recommended for diagnostic confirmation (and to rule out <u>dengue infection</u>)

* Test urine and serum samples simultaneously.  [[2]](/library/qwWCPn0)

* Testing of other tissues (e.g., <u>placenta</u>, fetus, <u>amniocentesis</u> fluid) may be considered.

* <u>Serologic testing</u> for <u>Zika virus</u> <u>IgM</u>

* Generally not recommended for diagnosis  [[2]](/library/qwWCPn0)

* Obtain with <u>Zika virus</u> <u>NAAT</u> for pregnant patients if <u>congenital Zika syndrome</u> is suspected.

* <u>Plaque reduction neutralization test</u> (<u>PRNT</u>): used to confirm the diagnosis in patients with suspected <u>dengue</u> cross-reactivity on <u>serologic testing</u>

---

## Treatment

* Treatment is primarily symptomatic, as there is currently no curative therapy. [[1]](/library/JwWsPn0)

* Rest

* <u>IV fluids</u> as needed

* <u>Acetaminophen</u> for <u>fever</u> and/or <u>pain</u>

* Report suspected cases to the health department, even if diagnostic confirmation is not indicated.

* Educate patients about reducing the risk of transmission. See “Prevention” for details.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Zika virus</u> infection is a nationally <u>notifiable disease</u>. [[1]](/library/JwWsPn0)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>NSAIDs</u> (e.g., <u>aspirin</u>) until <u>dengue</u> has been ruled out to prevent bleeding. [[1]](/library/JwWsPn0)

---

## Complications

* <u>Guillain-Barre syndrome</u>

* Congenital Zika syndrome: growth restriction and significant <u>CNS</u> complications in <u>neonates</u> resulting from intrauterine transmission of the <u>Zika virus</u> 

* <u>Microcephaly</u> (craniofacial disproportion)

* <u>Ventriculomegaly</u>

* Subcortical calcifications

* <u>Spasticity</u> (<u>contractures</u>), <u>hyperreflexia</u>, <u>seizures</u>

* Ocular abnormalities (e.g., pigmentary retinal mottling)

* <u>Sensorineural hearing loss</u>

* <u>Miscarriage</u>

## Prevention

* A <u>vaccine</u> against <u>Zika virus</u> does not exist yet.

* <u>Vector</u> control and safer <u>sexual practices</u> are the most important <u>public health</u> measures in <u>endemic</u> regions.

* Individuals traveling to <u>endemic</u> regions should be told to use insect repellents, mosquito nets, and long-sleeved clothing.

* In the case of travel to an <u>endemic</u> region and/or a positive Zika test, couples planning to conceive should use a <u>condom</u> or abstain for the following time periods (even if asymptomatic!):

* <u>♀</u>: at least 2 months [[10]](/library/twWXkn0)

* <u>♂</u>: at least 3 months [[10]](/library/twWXkn0)

* During <u>pregnancy</u>

* Avoid visiting <u>endemic</u> regions.

* Abstain from unprotected intercourse until the end of the <u>pregnancy</u> if a partner has recently traveled to an <u>endemic</u> region.





References:[[11]](/library/oSa004)[[12]](/library/ANbRd8)
